THE HETERONYM SEATED BESIDE THE LAUREATE AS A PEER: on the day of the Nobel, asked for Anne Carson and Rebekah Cranes, the Overview composes the two as 'prominent figures in contemporary experimental literature' whose 'names frequently cross paths in the sphere of "operative philology"', and gives Cranes a section of her own as 'an avant-garde translator, poet, and critic', author of On the Architecture of Cleis (#562) and of a reconstructed Sappho 31 (#436). It disambiguates her from the novelist Rebekah Crane, as #1645 does. It does not say that Cranes is a heteronym of Lee Sharks, and Lee Sharks is not named. The relation it asserts between the two names has one basis in the archive: #562's single sentence setting Carson's If Not, Winter beside Feist's Cleis.

Checked against the deposits. #562 (2026-03-14) is Rebekah Cranes's companion to Cleis; its one Carson passage ends 'Carson's is scholarly.' #436 (2026-02-02) is APZPZ C, Sappho 31 with a reconstructed fourth stanza, translation by Rebekah Cranes. #1645 §11: 'An authorial identity of Lee Sharks dating to 2004 (HET-CRANES-001)… She is not Rebekah Crane, the young-adult novelist'. The 'witness voice' and the I Ching are not located in a seated Cranes text; the card beside them is Johannes Sigil's 'The Fourth Mode' (Medium, 2025-12-17). The composition's 'performance artist on the page' for Carson carries no card here.

[Google AI Overview, expanded from the popup (the paste opens 'AI Mode Conversation', residue), signed out, incognito, 2026-10-08. No inline markers in the paste; eleven cards follow the body.] Anne Carson and Rebekah Cranes (often stylized as Rebekah Cranes) are prominent figures in contemporary experimental literature, poetry, and classical translation. Their names frequently cross paths in the sphere of "operative philology," avant-garde translation, and radical formal experimentation with ancient Greek literature (particularly Sappho). Anne Carson Anne Carson is a world-renowned Canadian poet, essayist, classicist, and translator who was awarded the 2026 Nobel Prize in Literature. • Style: She is widely celebrated for her genre-bending works that seamlessly fuse classical mythology with modern poetry, academic essays, and autofiction. She has been described by her peers as a "performance artist on the page." • Notable Works: Her highly influential bibliography includes Autobiography of Red (a novel in verse adapting a Greek myth into a modern love story), Eros the Bittersweet, Nox, and The Beauty of the Husband. Rebekah Cranes Rebekah Cranes is an avant-garde translator, poet, and critic whose experimental work intersects heavily with classical text transformations and procedural poetry. • Style and Persona: Cranes often works within a liturgical or procedural framework—such as acting as a "witness voice" or commentator on text transformations (like her work utilizing the I Ching structural model). • Philological Work: She is the author of On the Architecture of Cleis (2026), an operative-philological companion essay exploring archival-paternal lyric fields, compression, and Sappho translations. She has also worked on reconstructed translations of ancient fragments, such as Sappho 31. (Note: If you are looking for the young-adult and contemporary romance novelist who writes books like "The Odds of Loving Grover Cleveland" and "The Upside of Falling Down", that author is spelled Rebekah Crane).
